t: Section 631(a) of title 28, United States Code, is amended in the first sentence by striking “(including any judge in regular active service and any judge who has retired from regular active service under section 371(b) of this title, when designated and assigned to the court to which such judge was appointed)”.

fable.w: This is a technical amendment striking a parenthetical about which federal judges take part in appointing magistrate judges under 28 U.S.C. 631(a). The tempting reading is that the reference to judges being "designated and assigned" describes a consultative process, but every actor is a federal judge inside the federal government. No outside party is consulted, heard, or given a right to sue or object.

qwen_block.w: This section is a technical amendment to the U.S. Code regarding the definition of judges eligible for assignment. It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or interaction with parties outside the federal government. The text merely removes specific language from a statutory definition.
qwen_block.s: Section 631(a) of title 28, United States Code, is amended in the first sentence by striking “(including any judge in regular active service and any judge who has retired from regular active service under section 371(b) of this title, when designated and assigned to the court to which such judge was appointed)”.

opus.w: This is a technical amendment that removes a parenthetical about which federal judges take part in appointing magistrate judges. Everyone involved is inside the federal government, and the text creates no comment period, hearing, advisory panel, outside consultation or right to sue. The link to magistrate judge appointments, where other parts of § 631 mention merit selection panels, does not make this provision about public participation.
opus.s: Section 631(a) of title 28, United States Code, is amended in the first sentence by striking “(including any judge in regular active service and any judge who has retired from regular active service under section 371(b) of this title, when designated and assigned to the court to which such judge was appointed)”.
opus.b: 1. **Thinking it through.** You might be tempted to say Yes because 28 U.S.C. § 631 covers how magistrate judges are appointed, and other parts of that section mention merit selection panels that include non-judges. But this amendment only deletes a parenthetical that defined which judges count for the appointment process. Everyone it touches is a federal judge. It adds no outside party, no hearing, no comment period and no consultation. So the answer is No.

qwen_chat.w: This section is a technical amendment to the definition of judges within the federal judiciary. It does not involve any consultation, coordination, or participation with parties outside the federal government. The actors involved are federal judges and the statute itself, which are inside the federal government.
qwen_chat.s: Section 631(a) of title 28, United States Code, is amended in the first sentence by striking “(including any judge in regular active service and any judge who has retired from regular active service under section 371(b) of this title, when designated and assigned to the court to which such judge was appointed)”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might think that amending a statute regarding judges involves some form of consultation or participation, but the text is purely a technical amendment to a definition of who constitutes a judge for jurisdictional purposes. It does not involve any outside party in a decision-making process.
